title: Why debt interest now exceeds defence + schools combined
narrative_md:
**For the first time in peacetime history, the UK spends more servicing old debt than defending the country and educating its children combined.**

In 2023-24 the Treasury paid £105 billion in debt interest — more than the £57 billion defence budget and the £82 billion schools budget stacked together. A silent line item has become the single fastest-growing cost in the British state.

The numbers would have been unthinkable in 2020, when debt interest ran at roughly £25 billion and Bank Rate sat at 0.1%. What changed was not borrowing volume so much as borrowing price. Between December 2021 and August 2023 the Bank of England raised Bank Rate fourteen consecutive times to 5.25%, the fastest tightening cycle since the 1980s, and every basis point fed straight into the c.25% of UK gilts that are index-linked.

Compounding the pain is the Asset Purchase Facility indemnity. During quantitative easing the Treasury indemnified the Bank against losses on the £875 billion gilt portfolio. Quantitative tightening, begun in February 2022 and accelerated in 2023, now crystallises those losses — the OBR projects lifetime APF transfers from Treasury to Bank of roughly £150 billion.

Inflation-linked gilts were the accelerant. When CPI hit 11.1% in October 2022, indexation on around £600 billion of linkers repriced instantly. A single bad inflation print could add £7-8 billion to the annual interest bill, dwarfing any Treasury 'efficiency' drive.

Politically this creates a fiscal doom-loop. Chancellor Reeves's October 2024 Budget tightened fiscal rules to require debt falling as a share of GDP, but every 1% rise in gilt yields adds roughly £12 billion to interest costs. Defence — already under pressure to hit 2.5% of GDP by 2030 — and schools capital both compete directly with bondholders for what remains.

The UK is not alone, but it is unusually exposed: the share of index-linked debt is the highest in the G7, and the average maturity of gilts (14 years) means reset shocks take longer to fade. Debt interest is projected to stay above £100 billion annually throughout the parliament.

Every pound spent on interest is a pound not spent on a teacher, a nurse, or a frigate. That is the real cost of the 2020-22 fiscal experiment.
